t.1.75.1: Then Kāvya, the best of the Bhṛgus, filled with anger, approached Vṛṣaparvan as he sat, and without hesitation spoke thus.
t.1.75.3: Because you then had the brahmin Kaca Āṅgirasa killed, a man of sinless conduct who knew dharma, obedient and devoted to service, who delighted in dwelling in my house.
t.1.75.2: Unrighteousness that has been committed, O king, does not bear fruit at once, as the earth does not. If one does not see it in oneself, then it is in one's sons or in one's grandsons; evil surely bears fruit, like heavy food eaten in the stomach.
t.1.75.4: Because of the slaying of him who did not deserve to be slain, and because of the slaying of my daughter, understand this, Vṛṣaparvan: I shall abandon you together with your kinsmen. I shall not be able to stay with you in your realm, O king.
t.1.75.5: Ah, you take me for one who speaks idle falsehoods, O Daitya, since you do not restrain this fault of your own but simply overlook it.
t.1.75.6: Vṛṣaparvan said: I know of no unrighteousness in you, nor any falsehood, O Bhārgava; in you are righteousness and truth. Therefore may your honor be gracious to us.
t.1.75.7: If you abandon us and go away from here, O Bhārgava, we shall enter the ocean; there is no other refuge.
t.1.75.8: Śukra said: Enter the ocean, or flee to the far quarters, O Asuras! I cannot bear any unkindness done to my daughter, for she is dear to me.
t.1.75.9: Let Devayānī be appeased, for my very life rests in her. I am the one who secures your welfare, as Bṛhaspati does for Indra.
t.1.75.10: Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever wealth the lords of the Asuras possess on earth, O Bhārgava, be it elephants, cattle or horses, of all that and of me as well you are the master.
t.1.75.12: Devayānī said: If you, dear father, O Bhārgava, are master of the king's wealth, I do not acknowledge that of yours; let the king himself say so.
t.1.75.13: Vṛṣaparvan said: Whatever wish you desire, O Devayānī of the bright smile, that I shall grant you, even if it be hard to obtain.
t.1.75.11: Whatever wealth belongs to the lords of the Daityas, O great Asura, I am its master; if you would keep it, let Devayānī be appeased by you.
t.1.75.14: I desire Śarmiṣṭhā as my slave-girl, together with a thousand maidens; let her follow me wherever my father gives me away in marriage.
t.1.75.15: Vṛṣaparvan said: "Rise, O attendant, and quickly bring Śarmiṣṭhā here; whatever desire Devayānī wishes for, let her fulfill it."
t.1.75.17: Urged on by Devayānī, the brahmin is abandoning his disciples. Whatever wish she desires, that must be done by you today, O sinless one.
t.1.75.18: Whatever desire she desires, that I shall fulfil today; but let not Śukra, nor Devayānī, depart on my account.
t.1.75.16: Then the nurse went there and spoke these words to Śarmiṣṭhā: "Rise, good Śarmiṣṭhā, and bring happiness to your kinsmen."
t.1.75.19: Then, surrounded by a thousand maidens and borne in a palanquin, she hastily went forth from the excellent city at her father's command.
t.1.75.20: Śarmiṣṭhā said: I, with a thousand maidens, will be your slave and your attendant; I will follow you to wherever your father gives you in marriage.
t.1.75.21: To you I am the daughter of one who sings praises, a bard who accepts gifts; how then will you, the daughter of the one who is praised, become a slave?
t.1.75.23: When servitude had been promised by the daughter of Vṛṣaparvan, O best of kings, Devayānī spoke these words to her father.
t.1.75.22: By whatever means one can, one should bring happiness to one's distressed kinsmen. Therefore I shall follow you wherever your father gives you away.
t.1.75.24: I will enter the city, father; I am satisfied, O best of the twice-born. Your knowledge is unfailing, and yours is the power of learning.
t.1.75.25: Thus addressed by his daughter, that greatly renowned best of the twice-born entered the city joyfully, honored by all the Dānavas.
